programs.nl_rule:
The input grid has a black background with a single colored rectangle drawn in one non-black color. The rectangle is defined by solid border rows at the top and bottom, and solid border columns at the left and right, forming a grid-like structure. The interior is divided into cells by internal horizontal and vertical lines of the same color, with black cells filling the spaces between the lines. The rectangle can vary in size, position, number of internal divisions, and color.

Identify the rectangular structure and its top and bottom border rows. Let the bottom border row have distance d=0. For each row of the rectangle, compute d = (bottom_row - current_row). Shift the entire row's colored content horizontally according to d mod 4: if d mod 4 is 0, no shift; if d mod 4 is 1, shift left by 1; if d mod 4 is 2, no shift; if d mod 4 is 3, shift right by 1. Shifting means moving every cell in that row (both colored and the black cells between colored cells) by 1 position in the indicated direction. Vacated positions become black and content that moves fills its new position. All rows outside the rectangle remain unchanged.

The grid dimensions match the input exactly. The background is black (.). The colored rectangle occupies a contiguous region and is always axis-aligned. The grid is large enough that horizontal shifts of ±1 do not push content outside the grid boundaries.

Let me think about the rule carefully. The verifier: find vertical bounding box of non-zero cells (min_r, max_r). n = height. start = (3-n)%4. cycle = [0,-1,0,1]. For each row r in rectangle, offset = cycle[(r-min_r+start)%4]. Then shift nonzero cells; the row's colored content shifts but black cells between stay black (only nonzero cells shifted, and vacated positions become black—result initialized to 0). Actually since result is initialized to 0 and only nonzero cells are copied, the "black cells between colored cells" concept is same as just shifting nonzero cells. So the whole row's nonzero cells each shift by offset.

So offset for row index i (0-based from min_r): cycle[(i+start)%4] where start=(3-n)%4.

We want last row (i=n-1) to have offset 0: (n-1+start)%4 = index of 0 in cycle which is 0 or 2. cycle[0]=0, cycle[2]=0. (3-n)+(n-1)=2 → yes index 2 → offset 0. Good.

So the pattern of offsets down rows: for i, offset = cycle[(i + 3 - n) % 4].

tools.name: show_example

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

output_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.

tools.name: show_transformed_input

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Provide only an input grid. The environment applies the verifier and shows the resulting gold input-output pair to the student.

tools.name: query_student

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Probe the student with an input of your choice. You receive the student's predicted output, the gold output, and whether they matched. The student does not see the gold pair unless you later show it with show_example or show_transformed_input.

tools.name: start_exam
tools.description: End teaching and send the student to the exam: they must solve held-out generator inputs (unseen in demonstrations or probes) with the history so far. No further teaching after this.

tools.name: propose_inputs
tools.description: Submit candidate input grids you might show, several at once. The environment keeps the ones the verifier accepts, notes which leave the grid unchanged under the rule, and ranks the rest as candidates. Free: nothing is shown until you call show_transformed_input.

content.text:
We now have 7 demonstrations shown. That's good coverage: n=2,3,5,6,8 (and one from propose). We haven't shown a 7-row case? C3 n=7 was not in my 6? Let me check: I showed C1(n3), C4(n2), C8(n5), C7(n6), C5(n8), C2? Wait I showed 6: indices were C1, C4, C8, C7, C3(n7), C5. Let me recount from the calls: 1st call = C1 (n3 color1), 2nd = C4 (n2 color5), 3rd = C8 (n5 color2, 14 wide), 4th = C7 (n6 color9), 5th = C3 (n7 color4), 6th = C6 (n4 color7). 

Wait the 6th call input matches C6? C6 is n=4 7x7 block at row4-7 col2-8 color7 — no wait C6 was "n=4"? Let me re-check. C6 input: rows 0-3 zeros, row4 [0,0,7,7,7,7,7,7,7,...], row5 [0,0,7,0,0,7,0,0,7,...], row6 same, row7 [0,0,7,7,7,7,7,7,7,...]. So top row 4, bottom row 7, n=4, color7, 9-wide. Yes that's my 6th call actually... wait my 5th call was C3 (color4, n=7). Let me recount my six calls:

Call1: color1 n3 (C1)
Call2: color5 n2 (C4)
Call3: color2 n5 (C8)
Call4: color9 n6 (C7)
Call5: color4 n7 (C3)
Call6: color7 n4 (C6)

So I showed n=2,3,4,5,6,7. Missing n=8 (C5). Plus the one shown from propose (worst first) was some unknown. n_demonstrations went 2,3,4,5,6,7 — so first call resulted in 2 (1 from propose + 1). Good.

Could show n=8 too for completeness. Let me show C5 (n=8) to cover all heights. Actually n=8 gives offsets: bottom d0=0, d1=-1,d2=0,d3=+1,d4=0,d5=-1,d6=0,d7=+1. That's a good demonstration of cycle repeating.

Let me show C5. Then exam.
